newsitem.title: UK: Branson may make fresh attempt to circle globe.
newsitem.headline: Branson may make fresh attempt to circle globe.

text.p: British tycoon Richard Branson said on Thursday he might make another attempt to circle the globe in a balloon despite coming within 60 seconds of dying in a flight that went dramatically wrong just hours after take-off.
"I don't like to not finish a job. I suspect I would like to see the job done," he said when asked about a repeat voyage.
"It's great to be home and we've had the most fascinating and mixed 24 hours of our lives," the flamboyant entrepreneur told a news conference on his return to London.
Branson's daring round-the-world bid ended prematurely on Wednesday with a dizzying descent into the Algerian desert less than 24 hours after taking off from neighbouring Morocco.

The balloon's plunge was halted just 1,500 feet (500 metres), or 60 seconds, from the ground after co-pilot Alex Ritchie scrambled on to the top of the capsule to uncouple two ballast tanks to lighten the load.
"It would have been nasty if we had hit...the whole thing could have gone bang," Branson said.
Branson, who has flown across the Atlantic and Pacific oceans in a balloon, said that he had told himself during the unscheduled descent that he would not attempt a repeat performance if he survived.
But he admitted that the beauty of the landscape he saw when he landed and the thrill of the few hours in the air had made another trip seem tempting.
"Every time we come down he swears he'll never go up again," said Swedish pilot Per Lindstrand, clearly convinced Branson could be enticed into a fresh attempt on the record.
Lindstrand said that the sheer size of the balloon had made it difficult to steer.
"We encountered handling difficulties which I really can't explain 100 percent as I sit here," he said, adding that the balloon seemed very sensitive to temperature change.
Branson said he and Ritchie had thrown out food, water and oil and even a belt containing $2,000 dollars in emergency cash to reduce weight as they attempted to halt the balloon's fall.
"We were apprehensive," Branson said, with typical British understatement. "When you're heading towards the ground at 2,000 feet (600 metres) per minute you can't be entirely confident."
The Briton wished two rival teams well as they prepared to become the first to fly around the world in a balloon.
A Belgian-Swiss team is readying a launch from Switzerland in the next few days while American balloonist Steve Fosset intends to take off from St. Louis, Missouri.
Branson said he hoped the rivals got 99.9 percent of the way around the world.

Although not ruling out further adventures, Branson, whose Virgin group of companies spans a range of activities from airlines to insurance, said he intended to devote his attention to running his business for the moment.
"I'm back on the ground and back to business," he said.
